examples.problem_statement: Find the square root of 256 using prime factors

solution.description: 256 is even, so open the factor ladder with the smallest prime, 2; the division leaves 128.
128 is still even, so divide by 2 again, leaving 64.
64 is even, so the ladder continues with another division by 2, leaving 32.
32 is even, so divide by 2 once more, leaving 16.
16 is even, so divide by 2 again, leaving 8.
8 is even, so another division by 2 leaves 4.
4 is even, so dividing by 2 leaves 2.
The last 2 is itself prime, so dividing by 2 gives 1 and the factor ladder stops here.
Collect the ladder: 2 was used as a divisor eight times, so 256 is the product of eight twos, written compactly as 2 to the power 8.

solution.operation: Take square root of both sides
solution.description: Now apply the square root to both sides of that equality, so the root of 256 becomes the root of 2 to the power 8.
Halve the exponent, since taking a square root of a power divides its exponent by two; 2 to the power 8 therefore becomes 2 to the power 4.
Evaluate 2 to the power 4 by multiplying four twos together, which gives 16, the square root of 256.

examples.problem_statement: Find the square root of 196 using prime factors

solution.description: 196 is even, so begin the factor ladder with the smallest prime, 2; the division leaves 98.
98 is still even, so divide by 2 a second time, leaving 49.
49 is odd and divisible by neither 3 nor 5, so move up to the next prime that works, 7; the division leaves 7.
The remaining 7 is itself prime, so dividing by 7 gives 1 and the ladder ends.
Write out the divisors used, in order, to state the full prime factorisation of 196 as two twos and two sevens.

solution.operation: Pair identical factors: (2×2), (7×7); take one from each pair: 2 × 7 = 14
solution.description: Each prime appears exactly twice, so pair them and take a single factor out of each pair; multiplying that 2 by that 7 gives 14, the square root of 196.
